Annual Crop Land: Annual Crop Land shows a mosaic of rectangular and polygonal fields separated by sharp, straight boundaries.
Annual Crop Land often includes adjacent parcels with strongly different brown, tan, and green tones.
Annual Crop Land frequently contains bare-soil plots mixed with vegetated plots within the same field pattern.
Annual Crop Land has a fine, even texture inside each parcel rather than rough natural vegetation.
Annual Crop Land displays stronger geometric regularity than the broader, less structured grassy areas of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land lacks the repeated dot or row pattern of individual tree crowns seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Annual Crop Land usually has low vegetation cover that does not form the dense dark canopy typical of Forest.
Annual Crop Land is crossed by straight farm tracks or narrow roads aligned with field edges.
Annual Crop Land may show drainage or irrigation lines running parallel or perpendicular to parcel boundaries.
Annual Crop Land commonly forms medium to large field blocks with clear internal subdivision into smaller plots.
Annual Crop Land has crisp parcel edges that contrast with the softer, more irregular margins of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Annual Crop Land often alternates smooth plowed surfaces with lightly textured vegetated surfaces across neighboring plots.
Annual Crop Land tends to present a patchwork of cultivated units with little continuous unbroken green cover.
Annual Crop Land sometimes includes sparse building clusters or farm structures placed along plot margins or road junctions.
Annual Crop Land may contain narrow canals or ditches tracing straight lines between cultivated parcels.
Annual Crop Land usually shows managed vegetation arranged by parcel rather than the continuous spread of natural herbaceous cover.
Annual Crop Land often has lighter overall tones from exposed soil compared with the more uniformly green appearance of Pasture Land.
Annual Crop Land can include elongated strips as well as blocky fields, but the shapes remain clearly human-made.
Annual Crop Land shows neighboring parcels with contrasting crop height or surface roughness while each individual parcel stays uniform.
Annual Crop Land rarely contains large continuous water bodies, with water more often limited to thin linear channels along fields.
Highway or Road: Highway or Road appears as a long narrow corridor crossing the scene with fairly uniform width over long distances.
Highway or Road shows strong straight segments and sharp angular bends formed by engineered construction.
Highway or Road forms continuous connected lines that link intersections and branching junctions across built-up land.
Highway or Road is usually gray, white, or dark in tone and contrasts with greener or browner surroundings.
Highway or Road has a smooth homogeneous surface with little internal texture compared with clustered buildings.
Highway or Road remains a thin linear feature rather than a broad patch that fills a large parcel.
Highway or Road often runs in parallel with other transport lines or lane edges, creating paired straight boundaries.
Highway or Road differs from River by keeping more regular edges and avoiding obvious meanders and irregular banks.
Highway or Road differs from River by maintaining a more consistent width instead of widening and narrowing naturally.
Highway or Road often creates cross-shaped, T-shaped, or multiarm intersections with crisp geometric corners.
Highway or Road can appear as a network of straight corridors laid out in planned grids within urban areas.
Highway or Road is bordered by narrow roadside strips or scattered adjacent development while the corridor itself stays slender.
Highway or Road separates blocks or land parcels with clear linear boundaries rather than occupying them like buildings do.
Highway or Road has less tonal and textural variation inside the feature than Residential Buildings or Industrial Buildings.
Highway or Road may cut through vegetation as a distinct uninterrupted strip with sharp contrast against textured plant cover.
Highway or Road usually lacks the dense repeating small roof shapes that mark residential neighborhoods.
Highway or Road usually lacks the large rectangular roof masses and yard-like compounds typical of industrial sites.
Highway or Road appears more engineered and rectilinear than Herbaceous Vegetation Land, which is broader and more texturally mottled.
Highway or Road often extends from one edge of the scene to another, emphasizing corridor-like connectivity.
Highway or Road is visually defined by parallel elongated edges that guide the eye continuously through the landscape.
Forest: Forest shows large contiguous patches of dark green cover with soft irregular edges shaped by terrain rather than parcel lines.
Forest has a coarse mottled texture from overlapping tree crowns instead of the smooth uniform surface of herbaceous or pasture land.
Forest appears darker green overall than most crop or grass-covered classes, with frequent shadowed canopy pockets.
Forest lacks the straight internal boundaries and rectangular subdivisions common in annual crop land.
Forest does not show the evenly spaced row patterns typical of permanent crop land orchards or plantations.
Forest contains dense woody cover with little exposed soil visible between crowns.
Forest forms broad wooded blocks that are less fragmented into small fields than surrounding agricultural land.
Forest often follows ridges, slopes, and drainage corridors in irregular bands rather than a street-grid layout.
Forest has natural edges that feather into adjacent vegetation instead of sharply cut geometric borders.
Forest shows crown-scale texture variation with small dark and light spots, unlike the flatter tone of pasture land.
Forest includes very few roofs or paved surfaces, leaving the scene dominated by uninterrupted vegetation.
Forest may be crossed by only occasional narrow roads or tracks, which remain minor compared with the canopy cover.
Forest commonly borders streams or ravines with dense tree cover, while open fields nearby appear lighter and more uniform.
Forest presents layered canopy density that creates uneven shadowing, unlike the consistent brightness of herbaceous vegetation land.
Forest lacks plow lines, harvest striping, or other directional field textures seen in annual crop land.
Forest occupies larger natural patches, whereas confusable agricultural classes are often divided into repeated parcels.
Forest has rounded, clustered crown patterns rather than the linear plant spacing of managed perennial crops.
Forest usually contains minimal open water, and when water is present it is fringed by dense dark vegetation.
Forest displays a rougher and more vertically structured surface pattern than the fine grassy texture of pasture land.
Forest tends to connect into continuous wooded networks across the landscape instead of isolated small cultivated plots.
Industrial Buildings: Industrial Buildings feature very large rectangular roof blocks that occupy much bigger footprints than the small units of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings often appear as clusters of long warehouse halls separated by broad paved yards and loading areas.
Industrial Buildings show strong rectilinear geometry with sharp edges and regular parcel boundaries across the site.
Industrial Buildings are dominated by gray, white, or dark impervious surfaces with only sparse patches of vegetation.
Industrial Buildings have buildings spaced farther apart on larger lots than the dense, fine-grained pattern of Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings commonly connect to wide access roads and turning areas rather than appearing as only narrow linear corridors like Highway or Road.
Industrial Buildings include extensive parking or open storage surfaces that form large smooth paved zones around the main structures.
Industrial Buildings usually form compact industrial estates where multiple large roofs align in organized rows or blocks.
Industrial Buildings lack the repetitive striped texture of Annual Crop Land and instead show solid roof masses and pavement.
Industrial Buildings lack the orchard-like grid of Permanent Crop Land and instead present irregular clusters of large built volumes.
Industrial Buildings often create a patchwork of oversized roofs and paved aprons with minimal tree cover between them.
Industrial Buildings tend to have straight internal roads laid out in a functional grid around large building footprints.
Industrial Buildings present block-like structures whose width and length are both substantial, unlike the thin elongated trace of Highway or Road.
Industrial Buildings usually have fragmented vegetation confined to edges or medians rather than continuous green cover.
Industrial Buildings often occupy contiguous built-up parcels with abrupt boundaries between impervious surfaces and surrounding land.
Industrial Buildings can include a few retention ponds or water basins, but water is minor compared with the dominant roofs and pavement.
Industrial Buildings show low texture variation across roofs and yards, producing broad smooth surfaces instead of crop patterns.
Industrial Buildings frequently combine several massive halls with open maneuvering space, making the built area appear heavy and widely spaced.
Industrial Buildings usually have fewer curving streets and fewer tiny detached structures than Residential Buildings.
Industrial Buildings are characterized by dominant building masses embedded in paved compounds, not by agricultural rows, orchard dots, or purely linear transport features.
Permanent Crop Land: Permanent Crop Land shows large managed parcels with crisp boundaries and a consistent internal planting pattern.
Permanent Crop Land contains rows of evenly spaced woody plants forming clear parallel lines across each field.
Permanent Crop Land often appears as dot-like tree crowns arranged in a regular grid rather than a continuous canopy.
Permanent Crop Land has alternating bands of vegetation and bare soil or grass between planted lines.
Permanent Crop Land shows a more discrete and repetitive texture than the smoother cover of pasture or herbaceous land.
Permanent Crop Land displays organized row orientation that continues uniformly across an entire plot.
Permanent Crop Land includes rectangular or elongated fields whose internal texture is structured by planted rows.
Permanent Crop Land has canopy spacing that remains visible within parcels, unlike the dense unbroken cover of forest.
Permanent Crop Land often shows terraced or contour-following bands where woody crops are planted in repeated strips.
Permanent Crop Land contains internal farm tracks or straight service lanes aligned with field edges or planting rows.
Permanent Crop Land shows parcel-scale color variation organized by plot, with each plot keeping a regular woody pattern.
Permanent Crop Land often has medium-density vegetation cover with visible gaps between plant lines rather than full coverage.
Permanent Crop Land presents repeated clusters or lines of small crowns that create a checkerboard or comb-like texture.
Permanent Crop Land usually lacks the irregular patchiness of natural vegetation because the planting geometry dominates the parcel.
Permanent Crop Land can show narrow access roads dividing orchards or vineyards into orderly blocks.
Permanent Crop Land has field textures that remain stable and aligned, unlike annual crops that more often appear as uniform solid cover.
Permanent Crop Land may include scattered small buildings at field edges, while the planted parcels remain the dominant regular feature.
Permanent Crop Land sometimes borders irrigation ponds or channels, with water features serving geometrically arranged plots.
Permanent Crop Land shows stronger linear repetition within each field than pasture, which is usually more continuous and less banded.
Permanent Crop Land often combines muted green and brown tones in stripes or grids created by woody rows and inter-row ground cover.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land: Herbaceous Vegetation Land forms broad open patches of low vegetation with irregular natural edges rather than crisp rectangular field boundaries.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows a fine, even grassy texture without the dark coarse canopy pattern typical of forest.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is dominated by green to yellow-brown tones that are fairly continuous across the patch.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land lacks visible plow lines or parallel crop rows that would suggest annual cropland.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land does not show the repeated striping or evenly spaced planting points seen in orchards or vineyards.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land usually appears as open cover with few or no dense clusters of trees interrupting the surface.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has a soft, uniform surface texture rather than a strongly segmented mosaic of enclosed paddocks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often occupies medium to large contiguous areas instead of many small sharply divided parcels.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land contains little to no built structure, with no urban block pattern or dense roof clusters.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land is mostly uninterrupted by straight internal boundaries, unlike more managed pasture or crop fields.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land can include scattered narrow tracks or paths, but these do not create a rigid geometric grid.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land generally lacks bright bare-soil patches that would break up the vegetation cover.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land has a continuous low-cover appearance with minimal shadowing compared with woody vegetation.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land may include gently varying tones across the patch, but not the repetitive banding of planted rows.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land often borders other natural land covers with sinuous margins rather than fence-like straight lines.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land remains vegetation-dominated even near roads, without roadside building concentrations or industrial surfaces.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land shows no regular spacing of crowns or bushes, keeping the surface visually smooth and open.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land rarely includes water as a dominant element, and any ponds or channels occupy only small portions of the patch.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land appears less compartmentalized than pasture, with fewer clear subdivisions into separate grazing blocks.
Herbaceous Vegetation Land maintains an unmanaged-looking open cover pattern that is neither forested nor organized into crop geometry.
Pasture Land: Pasture Land forms large open parcels with clearly visible field boundaries separating one grassy enclosure from another.
Pasture Land usually appears in green to yellow-brown tones spread evenly across each field rather than mixed with strong bare-soil patches.
Pasture Land has a fine, soft vegetation texture that is smoother than the rougher natural patchiness of Herbaceous Vegetation Land.
Pasture Land lacks the repeated row geometry of Permanent Crop Land and instead shows broad continuous grass cover.
Pasture Land is more uniform across each parcel than Annual Crop Land, which often shows contrasting bands of soil and vegetation.
Pasture Land commonly has irregular to moderately regular field shapes that read as grazing enclosures rather than tightly cultivated blocks.
Pasture Land is an open landscape with sparse or absent tree cover across most of each parcel, unlike Forest.
Pasture Land often sits beside narrow farm tracks or rural roads that trace the edges of grassy fields.
Pasture Land shows contiguous agricultural patches with managed borders and fewer interruptions by dense buildings than urban land uses.
Pasture Land has vegetation cover that remains fairly even within a field, without the dense canopy shadows typical of Forest.
Pasture Land often includes hedgerow-like or fence-like boundary lines dividing adjacent grassy parcels.
Pasture Land presents a moderate parcel scale, with fields larger and more continuous than many small intensively planted plots.
Pasture Land rarely contains the tightly spaced dots or lines of tree crowns that characterize orchards and other Permanent Crop Land.
Pasture Land shows a consistent grassy surface where internal patterns are subtle rather than dominated by plow lines or harvest marks.
Pasture Land usually has low building density, with only occasional farm structures near field edges.
Pasture Land may include small ponds or drainage features, but water occupies only a minor part of the grassy parcel.
Pasture Land has smoother tonal transitions within fields than Herbaceous Vegetation Land, which often appears more mottled and uneven.
Pasture Land often appears as a mosaic of adjoining grass fields with coherent management patterns across neighboring parcels.
Pasture Land generally lacks the sharp seasonal contrast between bright vegetation and exposed earth that is common in Annual Crop Land.
Pasture Land maintains broad uninterrupted grassy expanses between roads and boundaries, emphasizing open managed ground rather than wooded cover.
Residential Buildings: Residential Buildings consists of many small to medium rectangular roofs packed into compact neighborhood blocks.
Residential Buildings is organized by short local streets and cul-de-sacs rather than a few broad transport corridors.
Residential Buildings shows a fine-grained mix of gray roofs, paved streets, and small green yards.
Residential Buildings has a regular parcel pattern with repeated house lots aligned along streets.
Residential Buildings contains scattered trees and lawn patches woven between buildings, giving a softer texture than industrial areas.
Residential Buildings forms dense built clusters with houses close together but still separated by narrow gaps and yards.
Residential Buildings has far less open paved area than Industrial Buildings, with roofs and yards dominating instead of large lots.
Residential Buildings presents a neighborhood street grid where roads connect building rows rather than overwhelming the whole patch like Highway or Road.
Residential Buildings lacks the long straight crop rows and broad uniform field blocks typical of Annual Crop Land.
Residential Buildings lacks the repeated orchard-like planting lines and evenly spaced woody rows seen in Permanent Crop Land.
Residential Buildings usually appears as contiguous blocks with sharp edges against surrounding vegetation or undeveloped land.
Residential Buildings shows numerous short driveways and small access links branching from residential streets.
Residential Buildings has a mottled texture from alternating rooftops, trees, and small open spaces rather than large single-use surfaces.
Residential Buildings often includes curved street patterns and cul-de-sac bulbs that break the rigid form of industrial compounds.
Residential Buildings is dominated by low-rise roof footprints that repeat frequently across the patch at similar scales.
Residential Buildings has internal roads that create many small blocks and parcels instead of a few massive structures.
Residential Buildings shows moderate vegetation embedded within the built area, not the broad continuous green of farmland.
Residential Buildings rarely includes large water bodies, and any water present is usually minor compared with the built neighborhood pattern.
Residential Buildings has building clusters that follow street frontages in rows, producing ordered bands of rooftops.
Residential Buildings appears denser and more geometric than natural land cover but finer and more fragmented than industrial estates.
Sea or Lake: Sea or Lake forms a broad contiguous water area that covers much more surface than a narrow river channel.
Sea or Lake has a smooth interior with very little texture compared with the fine grain of herbaceous vegetation land.
Sea or Lake is usually dark blue, blue-green, or gray across a wide continuous surface.
Sea or Lake has shorelines that create a compact rounded, lobed, or irregular basin rather than a thin meandering strip.
Sea or Lake lacks the rectangular field boundaries that often divide pasture land and other vegetated areas.
Sea or Lake contains no street grid or dense building footprints within the main water body.
Sea or Lake shows a much greater width-to-length ratio than a river, with open water dominating the shape.
Sea or Lake often has sharp edges where the water surface meets adjacent land or coastal margins.
Sea or Lake may include bright specular glint patches over part of an otherwise uniform dark surface.
Sea or Lake remains largely uninterrupted inside, without the frequent bars or bank divisions seen in river corridors.
Sea or Lake occupies a single expansive patch instead of many small parcels separated by hedges, fences, or tracks.
Sea or Lake has a nearly featureless center, unlike herbaceous vegetation land that shows mottled plant texture.
Sea or Lake may have irregular coves and peninsulas along the edge while keeping a wide open-water core.
Sea or Lake shows no parallel plow lines, grazing parcels, or other agricultural striping across its surface.
Sea or Lake appears as a coherent basin bordered by land, rather than a linear feature threading through land.
Sea or Lake commonly has a darker and more uniform tone than surrounding pasture land.
Sea or Lake can span the frame as an extensive open surface with only shoreline detail around the margins.
Sea or Lake lacks the branching drainage pattern and narrow connected reaches typical of river systems.
Sea or Lake presents broad open water with no dense canopy texture, distinguishing it from vegetated land covers.
Sea or Lake is defined by a large uninterrupted water patch whose outline is set by enclosing banks or coastlines.
River: River forms a long narrow water channel that crosses the scene rather than a broad enclosed water area.
River usually follows a sinuous winding path with repeated bends instead of the straighter alignment of roads.
River often shows branching tributaries that connect into a dendritic network of channels.
River has width that changes gradually along its course rather than staying uniformly constant like an engineered corridor.
River is typically dark blue, dark green, or gray and contrasts clearly with surrounding land.
River has smooth fine-textured water surfaces without the rough canopy texture of forest.
River is bounded by irregular natural banks rather than straight paved margins or lane-marked edges.
River commonly traces through the landscape as one continuous connected feature instead of many small separate patches.
River may include gentle meanders and oxbow-like curves that are uncommon in highways or roads.
River often has thin ribbons of vegetation lining both banks that follow the channel closely.
River can widen in some reaches and narrow in others while still maintaining an elongated channel form.
River lacks roof grids, block patterns, and other built-up textures within its main body.
River frequently occupies low-lying corridors with adjacent floodplain tones that parallel the channel.
River appears elongated across large distances, unlike a lake or sea that spreads outward in a wide basin.
River may split around small bars or islands before rejoining downstream in the same corridor.
River edges are usually uneven and organic, not the crisp parallel lines of a divided roadway.
River can appear darker in the center and slightly lighter near shallow margins along the banks.
River often intersects fields or settlements as a curving divider rather than following the regular geometry around them.
River lacks the dense, mottled, continuous tree crown texture that characterizes forest patches.
River tends to connect seamlessly to other waterways upstream or downstream instead of ending as an isolated water patch.
